extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, curriculum developers, and secondary/university mathematics instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for teaching, designing curricular materials, and researching classroom interventions that develop students' understanding and production of mathematical proof across K–12 and university levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof definition for instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem involves 'a proof if the teacher or students verified or demonstrated that the result must be true by reasoning from the given conditions to the result using a logically connected sequence of steps' (Hiebert et al., TIMSS 1999 Video Study definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this working definition when identifying proof tasks in lessons; avoid counting empirical demonstrations or example-based verifications as proofs. Example anti-pattern: treating repeated numerical examples as a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for student justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Student justifications should treat the general case and meet standards of proof rather than relying on empirical or case-based arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring/feedback should distinguish between empirical/particular-case arguments and arguments that establish generality via logically connected steps. Avoid positively evaluating non-proof empirical arguments as if they were proofs (observed in Bieda, 2010).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasks should promote conjecturing and generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof tasks ought to encourage students to consider individual cases, make conjectures, and develop arguments rather than present only known facts or teacher-model solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that invite student-generated conjectures and justification. Anti-pattern: sequencing tasks so students only memorize and reproduce teacher solutions (Sears, 2012 findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher role and orchestration
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers are central in deciding which proof-related tasks to implement and how, including facilitating student work without lowering cognitive demand and orchestrating whole-class discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective teacher actions include organizing activities, bringing together student contributions, responding to ideas in the moment, and providing feedback to sustain discussions. Common obstacles: weak knowledge about proof, beliefs that proof is for a minority, time constraints, and students' unhelpful habits of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher knowledge and beliefs about proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers need robust knowledge and productive beliefs about proof (e.g., seeing proof as a tool for communicating and studying mathematics, not merely a topic for a minority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional development and teacher-education materials should address teachers' conceptions; weak teacher knowledge and counterproductive beliefs correlate with marginal treatment of proof in classrooms (Knuth, Bieda, Sears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curricular/textbook design for proof
rubrics_metrics.description: School and teacher-education textbooks should provide coherent, sequenced, and conceptually grounded opportunities for students to engage in proving, address common misconceptions, and scaffold proving tasks across grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher guidebooks should offer practical advice for classroom implementation. Anti-patterns: limited/inadequately conceptualized place of proof in textbooks, poor sequencing, and lack of teacher-support materials (multiple textbook analyses cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment and evaluation criteria for proof
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for well-defined and consistent criteria to develop proving tasks and evaluate students' performance; different aspects of proof may require different criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment design should make proof salient (school/state/national tests) to influence textbooks and classroom practice. Current gap: lack of detailed examinations of how proof is treated in major assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: engineer cognitive conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional sequences can deliberately engineer cognitive conflicts to motivate movement from empirical reasoning to recognition of the need for secure validation methods (proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stepwise progressions and tasks that reveal limitations of empirical arguments so learners see an intellectual need for proof (Stylianides & Stylianides intervention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: make assumptions explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should become conscious of the role of hypotheses and axioms—proofs depend on explicit assumptions used to derive conclusions (Jahnke & Wambach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design contexts or historical/constraint-based settings where available methods/tools are restricted so students notice dependence on assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: progressive tool-to-theorem mapping (dynamic geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dynamic geometry environments (e.g., Cabri) can support the transition from intuitive to deductive geometry by progressively expanding available construction tools into theorems accepted by the classroom community (Mariotti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage software affordances while orchestrating classroom norms requiring justification before accepting new commands as theorems; teacher must purposefully organize activities and discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: guided reinvention and productive use of counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting imprecise definitions and allowing students to produce proofs and counterexamples can drive refinement of concepts and conjectures (Lakatos-inspired/guided reinvention; Larsen & Zandieh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat production and analysis of invalid arguments as integral to learning; use episodes where students face paradoxes to clarify definitions and hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: principled introduction of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach mathematical induction by highlighting the problems that motivate it and by deriving it from knowledge students already possess, rather than introducing it abruptly as abstract algebraic exercises (Harel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use problems that foreground recursive/process-pattern reasons for induction; sequence tasks so students move from empirical pattern noticing to transformational reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: target novice proof-comprehension behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions should address common novice tendencies (overfocus on algebraic features, linear reading of proofs) by training strategies like self-explanation to attend to logical relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, generic trainings (e.g., <20 minutes) on self-explanation improved undergraduates' proof comprehension and are scalable across settings (Hodds et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention scalability and practical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions that are short, generic, and require limited practitioner commitment are more likely to scale; long, resource-intensive interventions face obstacles to broader adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor designs that can be implemented with minimal curriculum overhaul and limited teacher preparation time (contrast longer multi-lesson interventions in some geometry studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research-practice linkage criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Research should connect (1) opportunities for proving in curricular resources, (2) classroom implementation of those opportunities, and (3) students' development of proving skills when using those resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future studies should adopt integrated designs that trace the pipeline from curriculum design to student outcomes to provide actionable guidance for teachers and developers (Cai & Cirillo recommendation).
